newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/preannouncements, PPI,CPI.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/preannouncements, PPI,CPI.

text.p: With the third quarter earnings season approaching, Wall Street will this week begin to focus on warnings of disappointing results.
Although some have already preannounced their earnings, the bulk of these warnings, expected primarily from high technolohy companies, will begin to pour into the market at the end of the week.

The week will also reflect a change of consensus concerning Federal Reserve action on interest rates with the Street now leaning towards the belief that the Fed will tighten in the wake of Friday's strong August jobs report.
The producer and consumer price indices, due Thursday and Friday, respectively, are not expected to play a major role in the Fed's decision nor are any upward surprises anticipated.

"The focus will be on whether we get any kind of downward guidance from corporate management on quarterly earnings," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line's Asset Management division.

"At the end of the week we'll be two weeks away from the end of the quarter and managements will know whether or not they have material problems. So far this quarter there haven't been any blockbusters that have rocked the market."
Of the 49 companies which have so far preannounced operating earnings for quarters ending August, September and October, the vast majority are negative, according to First Call Media Services.

Among the companies which have already issued warnings is Kellog Co which said the cereal price war sweeping through the country would trim third quarter earnings by about 20 percent from $1.05 in the year ago period.
At least four brokerages responded by lowering their earnings per share views on the company and shares sold off.

Wall Street's take on what the Fed is likely to do when its policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on September 24 has changed. Previously the consensus had been that the Fed would leave rates unchanged. But Friday's stronger than forecast August jobs report has changed that.
A rate increase, if it comes, would be the Fed's first such move in about 1-1/2 years.
"The consensus is that the Fed will pull the trigger and send rates higher by 25 basis points," Wachtel said. The PPI and CPI, he said, were not likely to influence its decision.
"It's the inflation that you don't see that the Fed wants to pre-empt. When it actually appears and the indices rise by 0.6 or 0.7 percent, it's too late to beat it back." he said.
"It's a rerun of 1994. The Fed will lean against inflation that is not yet seen, inflation which is still developing.
In addition to the PPI and CPI, data this week include Friday's August retail sales report.
